source_read: Publisher HTML (SAGE, free access; Aust N Z J Psychiatry 2018;52(6):514-529): structured abstract, Introduction, Method (incl. study design/extraction, quality assessment, synthesis), Results (study characteristics with Table 1, risk of bias within studies, results of individual studies with Table 2 and all risk-factor subsections, risk of bias across studies), Discussion (strengths/limitations, implications), Conclusion, conflicts, funding, publication information. Figures 1-2 are images; Online Appendix Table 3 (quality scores) and search-strategy appendices are .docx downloads and were not opened.

claims.overstatement: None in the claim's direction. Slight understatement: 'the level of use that carries risk could not be estimated' is true of thresholds, but this review grades the evidence that more frequent use goes with more psychotic symptoms as moderate (the only factor so graded), with a within-person dose-response in one cohort and 3- to 11-fold odds for more frequent use across four studies.
claims.note: This review compares users with and without psychosis (risk factors within users), so it does not supply or test the claim's user-vs-non-user pooled odds ratios (those come from McKetin 2019). It is consistent with the claim's symptom-versus-disorder pattern: frequency was associated with current symptoms in the higher-quality studies but not with lifetime substance-induced disorder or hospitalization outcomes. The authors state the literature is insufficient to support a causal association; the Discussion names seven papers (five populations) that did not exclude primary psychotic disorders, Table 1 indicates at least eight populations, and only six papers adjusted for other drug use.

anchors.locator: Abstract; Results > Patterns of MA use and Dose-amount and frequency of MA use; Table 2 (frequency row)
anchors.extracted: 13 study populations (20 papers; 5476 people). Frequency of use associated with psychosis in 4 studies (1503 people; mostly current-symptom outcomes) and not in 4 (2503; mostly lifetime-disorder or hospitalization outcomes); more frequent use estimated at 3-11 times the odds; dependence associated in 4 studies (2-3 times the odds). No meta-analysis possible because of heterogeneity. GRADE: moderate for frequency of use only; low to very low for all other factors.

Fewer than half of studies related current symptoms to current use; eight used lifetime outcomes. Mostly cross-sectional; seven papers (five populations) named as not excluding primary psychotic disorders (Table 1 shows more); only six adjusted for other drug use. Authors conclude the literature is insufficient to support a causal association.

claims.overstatement: None in the claim. This source misdescribes the comparison behind the 11.2 figure: it says people using on 16 or more days a month had 11.2 times the odds 'compared to those using less than 16 days', whereas the claim (and, per its predicted-risk figures, the primary study) compares months of 16+ days of use with months of no use. The claim's wording should follow the primary paper, not this review.
claims.note: Confirmed here: 278 methamphetamine-dependent people from outpatient treatment followed 3 years (past-month BPRS at 3 timepoints), lifetime schizophrenia/mania excluded, within-person design controlling for other drug use, OR 11.2 (5.9-21.1) for 16+ days. Not in this source: the any-use OR 5.3, the 1-15-day OR 4.0, the 7% and 48% predicted risks, and the further-adjusted 2.25 and 3.90. Additional qualification from this review's Table 1 (McKetin 2016 follow-up of the same cohort): transient symptoms associated with male sex, earlier onset of use, conduct and anxiety disorders; persistent symptoms with conduct disorder, anxiety, depression and family history of psychotic disorder. One of this review's authors (McKetin) led the primary study.

anchors.locator: Results > Dose-amount and frequency of MA use, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: One longitudinal study (McKetin 2013) controlled for confounders including other drug use and showed a within-subject dose-related relationship between days of use and concurrent psychotic symptoms; 16 or more days per month: OR 11.2 (95% CI 5.9-21.1), described as relative to fewer than 16 days.

Cohort; N=278 methamphetamine-dependent outpatients, 79% mainly injecting, 3-year follow-up; lifetime schizophrenia/manic episode excluded; BPRS past-month symptoms at 3 months, 1 year, 3 years; correlates: current frequency of use, concurrent cannabis and alcohol frequency; transient vs persistent symptom correlates listed; quality +++ (highest band).

key_findings.correction: The figures are as printed, but the review states the 11.2 compares people using on 16+ days a month 'to those using less than 16 days'; the card's 'than months with fewer' carries that comparator over without comment. The primary study's reference category is months without methamphetamine use (the claim's 7% to 48% predicted risks are no-use vs 16+ days), so this is a description error in the review that the card should flag rather than repeat.

reporting_issues.note: Table 1 study 9: 'not associated with MA dependence'; Table 2 dependence 'association' row cites 2, 9, 11, 12; studies 2, 11, 12 are all rated '+'.
Found independently; band pattern (+, ++, ++, +++) vs (+, ++, ++, +) confirmed from Table 1.
Spot-checked: gender 3657 and age 3949 reproduce only with study 3 as 79; polydrug 268 = studies 3 + 9; frequency-null 2503, dependence 1577 and family-history 912 do not reproduce.
Results > Patterns of MA use, 2nd paragraph.
Discussion lists Dawe 2013, Ding 2014, Kalayasiri 2009 and 2014, Lapworth 2009, Rognli 2014, Smith 2009 (five populations); Table 1 adds studies 1, 5 and 7.
Table 1 footnote: '+: total score 0-6; ++: total score 6-10'.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 low (one critical flaw: no excluded-study list).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: 'consistently' for a four-four split, and a causal-sounding Discussion sentence against an explicit no-causation limitation.

missed: The review's description of the McKetin 2013 comparator for OR 11.2 ('compared to those using less than 16 days') should be recorded as a reporting issue; it conflicts with the no-use reference used by the claim cl_meth_psychosis_dose.

Sulaiman 2014 (study 8) is listed in Table 1 as not associated with 'money spent on MA use', yet Table 2 and the text count it among the three studies in which greater amounts of use were associated with psychosis; same pattern as the Ding/dependence issue.
Table 2 personality row: 'Two studies found an association' for schizoid/schizotypal traits, while citing only study 6 and commenting 'Only one study assessed this'.

For cl_meth_psychosis_association: this review compares users with and without psychosis, so it cannot support the claim's user-versus-non-user odds ratios; its role is limited to qualifying (dose-related association with frequency graded moderate; causation not supported).
